title: Homology Roadmap
notes: Open the lecture by naming the conversion problem. The chapter turns a triangulated space into small integer matrices, then asks which closed chains survive after filled pieces are declared trivial. Point to the roadmap as the dependency chain students should keep in memory throughout the deck.

title: Oriented Simplexes
notes: Use the triangle to make orientation concrete before any algebra appears. An ordered simplex is not just a set of vertices; swapping two vertices changes the sign of the basis element. That sign convention is what lets neighboring faces cancel instead of merely accumulate.

title: Boundary Matrices
notes: Read the figure from left to right. The oriented triangle has three signed edge faces, so the D2 column is plus, minus, plus in the chosen edge basis. Then each edge contributes a minus at its initial vertex and a plus at its terminal vertex in D1.

title: Boundary Squared Zero
notes: This is the algebraic hinge of the chapter. If the boundary of a boundary were not zero, then boundaries would not automatically be cycles and the quotient definition would fail. The tiny triangle computation is not a special trick; it models the cancellation pattern in every dimension.

title: Cycles Versus Boundaries
notes: Keep the same red loop on both sides of the slide. In both complexes it has zero one-dimensional boundary, but only the filled triangle supplies a two-chain whose boundary is that loop. This is the first place where homology separates drawing a loop from detecting a hole.

title: The Quotient Definition
notes: Slow down here and name each group before computing ranks. Cq records every formal q-chain, Zq keeps the closed ones, Bq keeps the ones explained by a higher-dimensional filling, and Hq remembers the closed chains left over after those fillings are ignored.

title: Betti Numbers
notes: The rank formula is the computational contract for the chapter. Students should see that beta q subtracts two kinds of non-hole information: chains with visible boundary and cycles that are already the boundary of something higher-dimensional. The table entries are small enough to audit by hand.

title: Example Ledger
notes: Treat the plot as a quick diagnostic rather than a decorative chart. The interval has only one component, the circle boundary has one surviving loop, the filled triangle kills that loop, the wedge has two loops, and the tetrahedron boundary shifts the surviving hole into dimension two.

title: Euler Characteristic
notes: This slide gives the sanity check that prevents arithmetic from floating away from topology. Alternating simplex counts and alternating Betti numbers match in every example. Emphasize that Euler characteristic is coarser than homology, but it is an excellent error detector for these finite complexes.

title: Subdivision Invariance
notes: Subdivision adds many more simplexes, so it looks as if the matrices have changed the problem. The point is that the space has not changed. Direct attention to the new internal edges: each is produced twice with opposite orientation when the subdivided two-chain is bounded.

title: Cancellation Accounting
notes: Use the counts to make subdivision invariance inspectable. The original filled triangle has three vertices, three edges, and one face; the subdivided model has seven, twelve, and six. The Euler characteristic remains one, and the internal boundary coefficients are exactly zero.

title: Simplicial Chain Maps
notes: A simplicial relabeling should not merely send vertices to vertices; it must respect the boundary operator. The commutative square says that mapping a chain and then taking its boundary agrees with taking the boundary first and then mapping. That is the mechanism behind functoriality.

title: Maps Preserve Homology Classes
notes: Convert the commutative square into a proof in two lines. If a chain is a cycle, its image has zero boundary. If a chain is a boundary, its image is again a boundary. Therefore the map descends from chain groups to homology groups without depending on the representative.

title: Killing Loops Lab
notes: The lab is deliberately small: two triangular loops share a vertex, so beta one starts at two. Filling the left triangle increases the boundary subgroup by one and drops beta one to one. Filling both triangles leaves no one-dimensional homology class.

title: Lab Ledger
notes: Have students read each row as an experiment they could reproduce by editing a list of simplexes. The cycle space dimension stays two because the graph still has two closed edge sums, while rank B1 rises from zero to two as fillings are added.

title: Chapter Synthesis
notes: Close by putting the chapter back into one sentence: homology is closed chains modulo filled chains. The audit checks listed here are not peripheral; they are the computational form of the proof obligations students should demand from any simplicial homology calculation.
